paper_title: Multimodal Reranking Is a System One Decision

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal rerankers are usually dedicated models: a vision-language model (VLM) is trained on retrieval data to score the candidates of a query. Scoring options is not specific to reranking. System One decision models such as Jev map a state and a typed question to one probability per option without generating text, and general models can make such decisions with little or no training. Reranking is one such decision, with the query and its candidates as the state and the candidates as the options. We therefore argue that a general VLM can serve as a multimodal reranker through System One decisions, and that decision tuning can improve its reranking. We ask a VLM one choice question over the top 16 candidates of a first-stage retriever and rank the candidates by the probabilities of their labels, read from one forward pass. On MMEB-V2 image retrieval, this choice scores 5.4 to 7.3 hit@1 above a yes/no question per candidate, and the yes/no question falls below the first stage. With the choice, zero-shot Qwen3.8-27B beats the supervised Qwen3-VL-Reranker-2B on all three benchmarks and comes within 1.6 points of Reranker-8B on each. It matches Reranker-8B on MMEB-V2 visual documents (84.79 vs. 84.78 nDCG@5), at 1.1 to 1.5 times its latency. JEV-27B-VL, the same backbone tuned on text decisions only, improves page reranking by 0.6 to 1.1 points, with gains on most tasks (sign test, p <= 0.017), and leaves natural images unchanged. The zero-shot model is larger than the supervised rerankers and of a newer generation, so these comparisons are confounded; we discuss this and other alternative views, and the experiments that would test the position.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Multimodal retrieval usually ranks in two stages. first-stage retriever encodes the query and each item of the corpus, such as an image or page, independently into dense vectors and returns the most similar items as candidates. reranker then reorders the top candidates. Multimodal rerankers are usually dedicated models: vision-language model (VLM) is trained on retrieval data to read the query and one candidate together and output relevance score, for example the probability of yes [16, 17], or to rank several candidates at once [2, 5, 21, 33]. In this view, better reranking means training better reranker, and retrieval system serves the reranker as separate model. Reading score from the models output, rather than generating text, is not specific to reranking. System One decision models such as Jev [1, 10] map state and typed question to one probability per option, and are used for decisions of many kinds. General models can make these decisions: open language models serve as Jev-style decision models with little or no training, by reading the probabilities of option labels from the next-token distribution [10, 13, 18, 39], and VLMs make the 1 Figure 1: The choice readout. (1) The query and the top-𝐾 candidates of first-stage retriever go into one prompt under the labels AP. (2) One forward pass of vision-language model, with no decoding. (3) The next-token distribution, restricted to the label tokens and renormalized, gives one probability per candidate, and the candidates are reordered by it. Bar lengths are illustrative. same kind of decision when the state contains an image [3, 40]. Decision tuning, as in JEV-27B-VL [3], trains general model to make such decisions across tasks. Reranking is such decision: the state holds the query and its candidates, the question asks which candidate best matches the query, and the options are the candidates. We therefore take the position that general VLM can serve as multimodal reranker through System One decisions, and that decision tuning can improve its reranking. The position matters for two reasons. First, for deployment: retrieval-augmented systems often already serve large VLM to generate answers. If that model can rerank through one decision over the candidates, the system needs no separate reranker to train, serve and keep up to date. Second, for research: if reranking is one decision among many, it can improve with decision tuning across tasks, without reranking-specific training. The readout itself is not new: setwise prompting [42], FIRST [30] and ZipRerank [33] all rank candidates by the probabilities of their labels. What is open is whether general VLM can rerank this way without training for it. ZipRerank reports that zero-shot VLMs of 8B and 11B parameters, prompted as in RankGPT, do not consistently improve over the first stage [33], and zero-shot pointwise MLLM rerankers have helped only some query types [20] or not at all [12]. In our experiments the answer depends on the question type and on scale. One choice over all candidates improves the first stage on image retrieval, where yes/no question per candidate falls below it. Among Gemma 4 models, those of 12B parameters and more improve page retrieval zero-shot, and the two smaller ones lower it (Section 7.1). We test the position on MMEB-V2 image and visual-document retrieval [24] and on ViDoRe V3 [22], reranking the top 16 candidates of first-stage retriever. We first confirm on MMEB-V2 image retrieval that the choice format (Figure 1) outperforms the noul (yes/no) format asked zero-shot (Section 5), and use it in all following experiments. Two findings support the position. First, through one zero-shot decision, Qwen3.8-27B [28] beats dedicated 2B reranker on all three benchmarks, comes within 1.6 points of dedicated 8B reranker on each, and matches it on MMEB-V2 visual documents. Second, the same VLM tuned on text decisions alone reranks pages slightly better on most tasks, and natural images no better. These findings are encouraging but confounded. The VLM we test is larger than the dedicated rerankers and from newer model generation, so whether dedicated reranker built on the same backbone would do better remains open. Sections 9 and 10 discuss this and other alternative views, 2 and the experiments that would test the position. We release the code.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: System One models. TypeSafe introduced System One models with Jev, describing Jev as unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out and training it with reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions [1]; its weights and training method are not public [13]. Independent evaluations measured Jev on public text benchmarks [10] and in applications [15, 29]. Open reproductions read the same kind of decision from frozen language models: LLM-as-Jev scores numbered options with prefilled answer prefix [18], Releasing the Inner Jev reads letter logits at the last position and adds light LoRA recipe [13], and AnyJev divides out label prior and averages over cyclic option rotations [39]. Deußer et al. scored our backbone, Qwen3.8-27B, with this readout on text tasks [10]. In these works the options are mostly text. PixelJev [40] answers questions about an image with text options. Where the options are images, the model picks among few: the developers of JEV-27B-VL use it to compare two generated images and to rank up to eight short videos for recommendation feed [3, 37, 38]. Jev-style models have also been applied to text retrieval: re-ranking TREC-COVID [3], choosing among passages [7], and labelling data for passage reranker [31]. We rerank the images and pages returned by retrieval system, on retrieval benchmarks, and compare with supervised multimodal rerankers at the same depth. LLM rerankers that read logits. Zero-shot listwise reranking with LLMs started by generating permutations of passage identifiers [23, 26, 27, 32]. Setwise prompting showed that zero-shot model can rank small window of passages by the likelihood of their labels [42], and FIRST trained listwise reranker to rank by the logits of the first identifier token [9, 30]. In-context reranking reads attention weights [6, 8]. Pointwise rerankers read the probability of relevance label [25, 41]. In recommendation, listwise rerankers that read identifier log-probabilities show position bias [4]. Our readout is that of setwise prompting and FIRST; we apply it zero-shot to images and pages. Multimodal rerankers. Supervised multimodal rerankers score each pair with yes/no or relevance head [16, 17, 19] or rank several candidates jointly [2, 5, 21, 36]. Zero-shot MLLM rerankers have been used pointwise, where they help multimodal queries and hurt single-modal ones [20] or do not help at all [12], and listwise by generating permutation [11, 35]. Closest to us, ZipRerank trains VLM to rank pages by single-token letter logits in one forward pass [33]; its smaller zero-shot VLM baselines (Llama-3.2-11B-Vision, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct) do not consistently improve over the first-stage retriever. We use the same readout without training for reranking, on natural images as well as pages: zero-shot on larger VLMs than these baselines, and with decision head tuned on text decisions only (Section 3.4).

sections.title: 3 Reranking as a System One Decision
sections.content: Terms. For decisions we use the terms of Jev [3, 10, 18]. request has state, the context to judge, and typed question. choice question has set of options and returns one probability per option; noul question is yes/no question, answered with probabilities for false and true. For retrieval we use query and candidates, the items first-stage retriever returns for query. Table 1 shows how reranking decision fills Jev request under the two readouts we compare.

sections.content: The candidates enter the state in first-stage order, each introduced by its label, from Candidate A: to Candidate P:. For an untuned VLM, the state and the question form one chat prompt with thinking disabled (prompt in Section A). One forward pass gives the next-token logits 𝑧; restricting them to the label tokens ℓ1, . . . , ℓ𝐾 gives 𝑝(𝑐 𝑗 𝑞, 𝑐1:𝐾 ) = exp 𝑧ℓ 𝑗 𝑘=1 exp 𝑧ℓ𝑘 (cid:205)𝐾 , (1) and the candidates are ranked by 𝑝.

sections.title: 3.3 Yes/no readout
sections.content: The candidate is scored by the probability of yes against no at the first answer token, summing both casings of each (Section B). This is the readout of supervised pointwise rerankers such as Qwen3-VL-Reranker [17], applied zero-shot.

sections.title: 3.4 Two ways to obtain the probabilities
sections.content: We obtain the probabilities in two ways on the same backbone, Qwen3.8-27B [28], with the same state and question (Section A). Label logits of an untuned VLM. Qwen3.8-27B as released, with thinking disabled, read as in Sections 3.2 and 3.3; no weight is trained. We call this no decision tuning. trained decision head. JEV-27B-VL [3] is Jev-style decision model built on the same backbone: its developers add LoRA adapter and decision head to Qwen3.8-27B and train them on text decisions, leaving the vision encoder unchanged (Section B). We call this text decision tuning. No image enters the training, so every image decision JEV-27B-VL makes, ours included, is zero-shot for the decision head. The two models share every weight except the adapter and the head. Comparing them isolates text decision tuning, and comparing the two readouts on either model isolates the question type.

sections.title: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks. MMEB-V2 [24] image retrieval (12 tasks, hit@1) and visual-document retrieval (24 tasks, nDCG@5), with the task list, data loaders and metrics of the Qwen3-VL-Embedding evaluation code; ViDoRe V3 [22] (8 datasets, nDCG@10). For ViDoRe V3 we pool the queries of all six languages within each dataset and average over datasets. MMEB-V2 also has video retrieval tasks; we leave them out because JEV-27B-VL accepts no video input. 4 First stage. Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B [17]. All rerankers receive the same top-16 candidates. Models. Qwen3.8-27B and JEV-27B-VL are the controlled pair of Section 3.4; both run the choice readout on every benchmark and the yes/no readout on MMEB-V2 image retrieval. The dedicated references are Qwen3-VL-Reranker-2B and -8B [17], trained for reranking with pointwise yes/no score. Image budget. All models receive each image at most 1800 visual tokens (1800 32 32 pixels), the budget of the Qwen rerankers. Inference. All runs use one NVIDIA H200; Section gives the serving details.

sections.title: 6 Findings
sections.content: The two findings test the two parts of the position: general VLM reranks through System One decisions (Finding 1), and decision tuning can improve that reranking (Finding 2). Both use the choice format of Section 5.

sections.title: 7.1 Gemma 4 models
sections.content: We keep the main setup and replace the backbone with the five instruction-tuned Gemma 4 models [34], E2B, E4B, 12B, 26B-A4B and 31B, applying the choice readout unchanged and with no training. Gemmas chat template with thinking disabled also ends in an empty thinking block, and the labels AP are single tokens in its tokenizer. Two other things change with the backbone: Gemma 4 is different model family, and we keep its processors default of 280 visual tokens per image (the model supports up to 1120 [34]), against up to 1800 for Qwen3.8-27B (about 4.4k against 28.8k input tokens per ViDoRe V3 query). Within the Gemma 4 family the image budget is fixed; against Qwen3.8-27B, backbone, image budget and size all change. Figure 2 places each Gemma 4 model at its total parameters, 5.1B to 31.3B; 26B-A4B is mixture-of-experts model, so its total overstates the computation per token. Figure 2 shows the results. E2B and E4B lower the first stage on all three benchmarks. This is consistent with ZipReranks zero-shot baselines [33]. From 12B upward the readout improves visual-document retrieval, by 1.7 to 2.9 nDCG@5 on MMEB-V2 visual documents and by 2.4 to 3.4 nDCG@10 on ViDoRe V3; on natural images only 31B improves the first stage, by 2.6 hit@1. sections.title: 8.1 Where the choice helps
sections.content: Finding 1 rests on benchmark means. The choice readout on Qwen3.8-27B improves the first stage by 1.9 hit@1 on natural images, by 5.6 nDCG@5 on MMEB-V2 visual documents and by 7.9 nDCG@10 on ViDoRe V3  (Table 3)  . Over the 12 image tasks  (Table 7)  it gains on all nine tasks whose query contains text: most on CIRR (+7.1 hit@1), whose queries combine an image with modification text, then on Wiki-SS-NQ (+3.8), VisDial (+3.3) and FashionIQ (+3.1), and by 1.6 to 2.8 points on the other five. It loses on the three tasks whose query is an image alone: MSCOCO image-to-text (4.1), VisualNews image-to-text (1.7) and NIGHTS (0.7); two of them retrieve captions and one retrieves images. JEV-27B-VL loses on the same three tasks. MM-Embed found that zero-shot pointwise reranking with True/False readout helps multimodal queries and lowers accuracy on single-modal queries [20]. With the choice readout, single-modal text queries gain as well, and the losses are confined to image-only queries.

sections.title: 8.2 Why the choice beats the yes/no format
sections.content: The choice compares the 16 candidates in one context, and their probabilities sum to one. The yes/no readout scores each candidate in separate prompt, and nothing places the 16 probabilities on shared scale. We hypothesize that this is why the zero-shot yes/no readout falls below the first stage: ranking needs scores that are comparable across candidates, and supervised pointwise rerankers such as Qwen3-VL-Reranker are trained for reranking with this readout, while general VLM is not. The same ordering of the two question types appears for short videos in recommendation feed: the developers of JEV-27B-VL report that, on 200 cases built from public playlists, each with 20 candidates, one choice question per batch reached AUC 0.931 against 0.905 for one yes/no question per candidate [37].

sections.title: 9 Alternative Views
sections.content: We state the views that most directly challenge the position or the findings that support it, and how far our results answer them. AV1: Stronger VLMs make stronger dedicated rerankers too. Qwen3-VL-Reranker is trained from Qwen3-VL, and stronger VLM is also stronger backbone for dedicated reranker. Our comparison sets zero-shot 27B model against supervised 2B and 8B models of different generation, so it changes supervision together with scale and generation. It shows that zero-shot VLM can match dedicated 8B reranker on MMEB-V2 visual documents today, not that it would match dedicated reranker trained from the same backbone; JEV-27B-VL, the best reranker on both visual-document benchmarks, inherits the same confound. This view limits the practical value of the general route; Section 10 describes the test. AV2: general VLM is too expensive. This view qualifies Finding 1. Qwen3.8-27B has more than three times the parameters of Reranker-8B and needs more GPU memory, and its latency per query is 1.1 times that of Reranker-8B with the released code and 1.5 times with batched scoring (Section 7.2). In favor of the position, as argued in Section 1, system that already serves VLM could rerank with the same model. AV3: Small models cannot do it. This view also qualifies Finding 1. Small general VLMs lower the first stage (Section 7.1), so Finding 1 holds only for sufficiently large models, and at small sizes dedicated model is ahead today: Reranker-2B improves both visual-document benchmarks, where Gemma 4 E2B and E4B lower them. 8 AV4: Dedicated listwise rerankers already exist. This view questions what is new in the position. ZipRerank [33] trains for reranking with the readout we use (Section 1). Our position is that decision tuning can also produce good reranker, and the two routes can coexist. Under ours, model tuned on many kinds of multimodal decisions, of which reranking is one, should approach dedicated listwise reranker on reranking while keeping its other decisions. AV5: The readout has practical limits. This view concerns the choice readout. One prompt holds at most 16 candidates under the labels AP, while the published Qwen3-VL-Reranker numbers rerank the top 100. Deeper lists could be reranked with sliding windows [32] or with repeated choices over small sets, as in setwise sorting [42], at one prefill per window or set; the decision endpoint of JEV-27B-VL also extends its labels beyond with no retraining [3]. Listwise readouts depend on option order [14, 39] and prefer some labels whatever the input [39], and we present the candidates in first-stage order only. These limits matter for deployment, but they are properties of the readout rather than arguments for dedicated model: listwise LLM rerankers in recommendation show position bias as well [4].

sections.title: 10 Testing the Position
sections.content: Multimodal decision tuning. Tune VLM on decisions of many kinds that include visual options: ranked list with relevance labels gives choice questions over images and pages, and two candidates of different relevance give preference question. The position is refuted if this tuning does not improve the VLMs reranking, in particular on natural images, where text decision tuning does not help, and on queries that are an image alone, where the choice readout loses (Section 8.1). The gap on one backbone. On one VLM at several sizes, compare the zero-shot choice, the same model after multimodal decision tuning, and dedicated reranker trained from it. gap to the dedicated reranker that shrinks with size strengthens the general route; gap that persists supports AV1 and limits the routes practical value. Backbone and image budget. Run Qwen3.8-27B at the image budget of Gemma 4, or Gemma 4 at larger one. This tells whether the gap between the two families in Section 7.1 comes from the backbone or from the image budget. The choice readout. Measure how the choice probabilities change with the order of the candidates (AV5) and how well they are calibrated, and correct for order, for example by averaging over cyclic rotations [39]. Order effects that dominate the ranking would weaken the choice format as the interface of general reranker.

sections.title: 11 Conclusion
sections.content: Multimodal rerankers are usually dedicated models. We argued that general VLM can serve as multimodal reranker through System One decisions, and that decision tuning can improve its reranking. On MMEB-V2 image retrieval, one choice question over the candidates scores 5.4 to 7.3 hit@1 above yes/no question per candidate, and the yes/no question falls below the first stage. With the choice, zero-shot Qwen3.8-27B beats the supervised Qwen3-VL-Reranker-2B on all three benchmarks, comes within 1.6 points of Reranker-8B on each, and matches it on MMEB-V2 visual documents, at 1.1 to 1.5 times its latency. The same backbone tuned on text decisions only improves page reranking by 0.6 to 1.1 points, with gains on most tasks, and leaves natural images unchanged. The zero-shot model is larger than the supervised rerankers and of newer generation, so these comparisons are confounded. If the position holds, multimodal decision tuning offers route to better multimodal reranking alongside dedicated rerankers; Section 10 lists the experiments that would tell.

sections.title: B Implementation details
sections.content: Reading the label probabilities. Let 𝑥 be the token sequence of prompt A, rendered by the chat template with thinking disabled and ending where the answer starts, and let 𝑧 = 𝑓 𝜃 (𝑥) be the next-token logits at that position. With label tokens ℓ1, . . . , ℓ𝐾 (the single tokens A, B, . . . ; ids 32 to 47 in the Qwen3.8 tokenizer), candidate 𝑐 𝑗 receives 𝑝 𝑗 by Equation (1). The yes/no readout of prompt uses the tokens yes, Yes, no, No (ids 9405, 9175, 2083, 2665) and scores candidate by 𝑃(yes) = 𝜋yes + 𝜋Yes 𝜋yes + 𝜋Yes + 𝜋no + 𝜋No , 𝜋𝑤 = exp 𝑧𝑤. (2) 14 Both read single forward pass; nothing is decoded. Obtaining the logits from vLLM. Each prompt is one chat-completion request with the fields of Table 6. The server runs with --logprobs-mode processed_logprobs, so the returned log-probabilities are those of the distribution after the allowed-token mask, and the explicit sampling parameters keep the models default sampling settings from truncating it. The client applies softmax to the 𝐾 returned values, which gives Equation (1); the sampled token is not used. Table 6: The chat-completion request behind prompts and B.

sections.content: autotrust/JEV-27B-VL (served with the unmodified Qwen3.8-27B weights) one user turn with the parts of prompt or 1 the label tokens: A, . . . , ℓ𝐾 (ids 3247), or yes, Yes, no, No true, the number of label tokens true 1, 1, 0 {"enable_thinking": false} In all 14,419 choice requests to Qwen3.8-27B, every one of the 230,704 labels received log-probability. JEV-27B-VL. Its developers train the LoRA adapter and the decision head on the jev-distill-corpusv3 dataset of text decisions; the tuned head answers noul questions, choice questions with 2 to 256 options and 05 ratings. On held-out rows of that dataset labelled by TypeSafes Jev 1.13, the model card reports KL divergence of about 0.017 from Jevs output distributions. The endpoint /v1/decide takes the state, the question and, for choice, the options, and returns one probability per option from one forward pass. The same state and question as for Qwen3.8-27B go to this endpoint (prompt C). Its decision head returns one probability per option, and these probabilities are 𝑝 𝑗. For the yes/no readout, request whose question type (the field kind) is noul returns probabilities for false and true; we use the second. Ranking. Candidates are sorted by 𝑝 𝑗 in decreasing order, ties broken by first-stage rank, and candidates below the top 𝐾 keep their first-stage rank. query whose request fails would keep the first-stage order; no request failed in any run reported here. Inputs. Images are converted to RGB and, when larger than 1800 32 32 = 1,843,200 pixels, downscaled with bicubic resampling at the same aspect ratio; they are sent as JPEG data URLs (quality 90), and the servers image processor then resizes them as it does any input. Runs of whitespace in text are collapsed to one space. The choice prompts are about 3.1k tokens long on MMEB-V2 image retrieval, 17.8k on visual-document retrieval and 28.6k on ViDoRe V3. Serving. Both 27B models are served by the server in the JEV-27B-VL repository (model revision fee8c1d) on vLLM 0.30.0, started as below. Chat requests for the served name autotrust/JEV-27B-VL use the unmodified Qwen3.8-27B weights; /v1/decide adds the LoRA adapter and the decision head. The client keeps 8 queries in flight; the yes/no readout sends the 16 requests of query one after another. Server command (one H200) python3 JEV-27B-VL/serve_decide.py --model JEV-27B-VL --served-model-name autotrust/JEV-27B-VL --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 32 --lora-modules jev-decision=JEV-27B-VL/adapter_vllm --logprobs-mode processed_logprobs --max-model-len 65536 --enable-prefix-caching --mamba-cache-mode align --max-num-seqs 8 --trust-request-chat-template --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": 80}' # 20 on ViDoRe V3 Supervised rerankers. Qwen3-VL-Reranker-2B (revision 4bd860a) and -8B (b212dc8) run with the released code of the Qwen3-VL-Embedding repository at commit 393e297, in bf16 with FlashAttention-2: on MMEB-V2 through the repositorys reranker evaluation, and on ViDoRe V3 through the same reranker class (prompt D). The class scores the 16 pairs of query one after another, truncates each pair to 10,240 tokens and caps each image at 1800 32 32 pixels. Its score is 𝜎 (cid:0)(𝑤yes 𝑤no)ℎ(cid:1), with ℎ the last hidden state and 𝑤 rows of the language-model head, which equals 𝜎(𝑧yes 𝑧no). Under transformers 5.8, one-line patch rebuilds the processors mm_token_type_ids from the final input ids; under transformers 4.57 it changes nothing. First stage. Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B (revision 9f2f7e7). On MMEB-V2 we run the repositorys embedding evaluation, whose rankings its reranker evaluation reads. On ViDoRe V3 we use the same embedding class: pages with its default instruction, queries with the instruction of Table 5, and the top 100 pages by the inner product of the returned embeddings. Metrics. MMEB-V2 uses the repositorys ranking metrics: hit@1 for image retrieval and ndcg_linear@5 for visual documents, averaged over tasks. For ViDoRe V3, with graded relevance 𝑔 from the qrels and ranking 𝑟, nDCG@10 = DCG/IDCG, where DCG = (cid:205)10 𝑔(𝑟𝑖)/log2(𝑖 + 1) 𝑖=1 and IDCG is the same sum over the ten largest positive gains. It is computed per dataset over the queries of all six languages and averaged over the eight datasets. Hardware and software. One NVIDIA H200 per run. The Qwen models run with torch 2.8, transformers 5.8 and flash-attn 2.7.3; the 27B models run on vLLM 0.30.0.
